messages.subject: Rescaling
parts:
In order to identify an IRT model I’m working on, I’m experimenting with the scaling and normalizing approach from ARM (and cribbing from https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/feature/ARM/src/models/ARM/Ch.19/item_response.stan)

I note that there’s a typo in that example (and the book!), in that scale and shift are defined in terms of ‘a', not ‘a_raw'. The model won’t even compile in Stan as written. OTOH, being able to rescale a parameter would address my questions below (e.g., by simply declaring a ~ normal(mu_a,sigma_a); a <- (a-mean(a))/sd(a);)

More importantly, it runs fairly slowly and returns samples for all the intermediate parameters, parameters that AFAIK can’t really be interpreted meaningfully. a_raw, b_raw, and g_raw don’t matter, except for computational convenience; we only really need a, b, and g. But sampling them and reporting them chews up memory and CPU (as I understand how Stan works). Is there a way to prevent those intermediate variables from being reported back to R, and to optimize how they’re handled internally? Ideally, they’d be local variables in the model, but I don’t think there’s a way to refactor the model to make that happen.

Indeed, I wonder if the redundant parameterization trick is as powerful in Stan as it would be in BUGS. As I understand it, that approach helps in BUGS because each parameter is updated separately, while they’re all updated at once in Stan, so the sort of drift described in ARM chapter 19 can’t happen, and redundant parameterization shouldn’t speed things up (in which case I’d do just as well at identifying the model by constraining various priors).

Am I understanding the various issues involved clearly, or have I failed to grok some essential truth about Stan?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Rescaling
parts:
On Mar 23, 2014, at 6:44 AM, Joshua Rosenau <josh.r...@gmail.com> wrote:

> In order to identify an IRT model I'm working on, I'm experimenting with the scaling and normalizing approach from ARM (and cribbing from https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/feature/ARM/src/models/ARM/Ch.19/item_response.stan)
>
> I note that there's a typo in that example (and the book!), in that scale and shift are defined in terms of 'a', not 'a_raw'. The model won't even compile in Stan as written.

Is there a model we've used as an example somewhere that doesn't compile? If
so, we need to fix it. the item-response example linked above compiles OK.

> OTOH, being able to rescale a parameter would address my questions below
> (e.g., by simply declaring a ~ normal(mu_a,sigma_a); a <- (a-mean(a))/sd(a);)

I'm not sure what you mean here in terms of execution order. If you want to redefine
a in the model, it needs to be a local variable.

If you transform a first and then put it on the left of a sampling statement,
you need to account for the Jacobian of the transform.

What you could do is use the unit_vector[K] type, which constrains the
elements in the vector to have mean 0 and variance 1, and takes care of
the Jacobian internally.

> More importantly, it runs fairly slowly and returns samples for all the intermediate parameters, parameters that AFAIK can't really be interpreted meaningfully. a_raw, b_raw, and g_raw don't matter, except for computational convenience;

The raw forms are what the HMC sampler is actually sampling,
after transforms that unconstrain all variables. So in terms of
diagnosing issues with the sampler itself, they're what you need
to focus on. They're also what you need to watch to monitor convergence
and mixing.
> we only really need a, b, and g.
Right --- that's what you're going to use for inference.
> But sampling them and reporting them chews up memory and CPU (as I understand how Stan works).

Not CPU so much. The raw parameters are what's being sampled and
the transforms have to be done to expose the parameters in the model.
So there's no overhead. It does chew up memory in RStan if you're
saving a large number of samples. (8 bytes per parameter per sampling
iteration.) It doesn't chew up memory in CmdStan, because it streams, but
will chew up memory in posterior diagnostics from bin/print.
> Is there a way to prevent those intermediate variables from being reported back to R, and to optimize how they're handled internally?

The only internal optimization is that they don't get printed.
All the computations have to happen in terms of the declared
parameters for sampling and conversion for use in the model.

But I think there's a way in RStan to limit the parameters that
are reported. Look at the pars value in stan() --- you can use
it to list the parameters you want to save.

We'd recommend monitoring all the parameters (default without a pars
value) until you're sure the model's well-behaved in terms of convergence.
> Ideally, they'd be local variables in the model, but I don't think there's a way to refactor the model to make that happen.

No, you can't do that refactoring in the model unless you
can analytically marginalize a parameter out.

Whenever you can do that, it's a very good idea for computation.
Even if you can sample the parameter, it's almost always more efficient
in terms of inference to use an analytical marginalization.

> Indeed, I wonder if the redundant parameterization trick is as powerful in Stan as it would be in BUGS. As I understand it, that approach helps in BUGS because each parameter is updated separately, while they're all updated at once in Stan, so the sort of drift described in ARM chapter 19 can't happen, and redundant parameterization shouldn't speed things up (in which case I'd do just as well at identifying the model by constraining various priors).
>
> Am I understanding the various issues involved clearly, or have I failed to grok some essential truth about Stan?

I'll let you decide that! The thing to read is chapter 21 of
the manual, chapter "Execution of a Stan Program". It goes
through all the data moves and transforms and I/O.

- Bob
>
